title: Subway: Build the City, Break the Budget
subtitle: A quick look at the strategy hiding inside the Subway board game
description: A short Build Radio test episode about strategy in the Subway board game.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: This is Build Radio. Today we're looking at Subway, a board game where players build competing transit networks across a city. At first it looks like a route-building puzzle. Underneath that, though, there's an economy game.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Exactly. Every station, turn, crossing, and connection is really a capital allocation decision. You're not just asking where your line should go. You're asking what is worth paying for now.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: And players can go into debt, which creates an interesting endgame strategy.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Debt changes the tempo. Early debt can hurt because you carry the downside for a long time. But if you're close to finishing a valuable line, taking on debt for one huge construction turn can make sense. You're effectively borrowing against victory points.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Then there are shared stations and crossings. Using another company's infrastructure costs money, but avoiding it might force a longer route.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Which creates the interesting part: the cheapest network is not necessarily the best network. Players are balancing objectives, connectivity, construction speed, cash, and global bonuses like longest network and largest transfer station.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: So Subway isn't really about drawing lines. It's about deciding when efficiency matters, when expansion matters, and when it's worth spending tomorrow's money today. That's Build Radio.
